Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

crimlab 0.0.3

  • No function changes. The command-line build can lower the compiler flags of its JSON layer alone (JOPT), which the Fedora package does on riscv64: that one file took the emulated builders over an hour, and the packages of 0.0.2 were not built there.

crimlab 0.0.2

  • The fits of ppmlfe(), ivfe(), ppmlcf(), expgmm(), fepnl(), gmmpnl(), didfe(), rdloc() and sarml() answer to the usual accessors: coef(), confint(), vcov() and nobs() (help page racc). The intervals are the fit’s own, at its own level.

  • A file written under a name with no suffix is given one: wrtxtfb() adds .txt, and yoycsv(), yoytsv(), yoyjs(), yoymd(), yoyhtml() and yoypdf() the suffix of their format. Each returns the path it wrote.

  • The rOpenSci standards notes describe the package as it is now: the regression standards are documented (src/srrre.h), the general and spatial notes written when the package was small are brought up to date, every internal R function has a roxygen comment, and tests/README.md says how the full test suite is switched on.

  • The argument that names a method is mthd (it was meth), and so is the part of a result that records it: in lodimp(), stgdid(), wcbx(), sarml(), cortbl(), topcors(), evfilt(), scboot(), chomap(), smmap() and co2fp(), in R and in every other language. A call that names the old argument is refused.

  • Plots are black and grey on a white ground with a black frame and a bold title, as a journal prints them: the tinted panel and its grid are no longer the default. plotopt(palette = "okabe") brings the colours back, and plotopt(grid = TRUE, panel = "#EEF1F6") the panel and grid. The "grey" palette starts at black and has no grey too pale to read on white.

  • Intervals are drawn with a cap at each end. plot() of evtst() and stgdid() with pal = "diverging" is blue before adoption and red after. plot() draws the power curve of wcbx(mthd = "power"). plotevgrid(x, style = "stata"), and plot() of evtst() and stgdid() with it, draws hollow points joined by a line with dashed intervals. The Goodman-Bacon panel of plot(didfe()) names the two-way estimate its line marks.

  • New functions for the review of restrictive confinement, after the analyses of Sprott and Doob (2021) and of Sprott, Doob and Iftene (2021) of Canada’s Structured Intervention Units, in R and in every other language. rvwtim(): whether a review due by a set day was held, the stays past that day never reviewed, and how long the reviews held took. entcmp(): the days of a stay on which an entitlement (hours out of cell, human contact) was missed, by how often, with the hours received on those days and the part refusals account for. dmvar(): whether decision makers decide alike, with each one’s rate, the chi-square test, and the test with the small ones and with each one left out.

  • New plots. plot() of wcbx(mthd = "perm") draws the permuted statistics of each outcome with the observed one, as a histogram or a density (the result now keeps them, as null, in every language). plot(didfe(loo = TRUE), type = "hist") draws the leave-one-out estimates as a histogram with a summary. plotcoh() draws the mean outcome of each adoption cohort around its adoption, and returns the points in every language. plot() of yoypx() with what = "value" draws the values over the periods.

  • The command-line program and the library are built with the arithmetic of SSE2 on 32-bit x86, as every other platform computes. With x87 arithmetic and a distribution’s options (link-time optimisation, no frame pointer) three results of the test table differed in their last digits, and the openSUSE i586 package of 0.0.1 failed its checks. A build that names -mfpmath itself keeps its choice.

  • A check of CRAN runs one test file, the compiled self-test of every kernel and one call of every exported function; the whole suite, which takes minutes, runs in the project’s own checks on every push (NOT_CRAN=true).

  • The package installs faster: R compiles its C++ sources in 40 groups (a unity build, src/u_*.cpp) and no longer one file at a time, so the headers are read 40 times, not 337. Nothing a caller sees changes.

  • Outside R the plots are drawn too. plotsvg() (Python, Go, Rust, Java, JavaScript and the command line) runs a plot function on its arguments and returns the picture as a standalone SVG document with the rows drawn: plotlrnz(), plotgain(), plotcdfs(), plotrdg(), plotvln(), plothex(), plotfnl(), plotcal(), plotmult(), plotbump(), plothrz(), plotevgrid() and plotcoh(), and every result R draws with plot() (evtst(), stgdid(), synthc(), sdidx(), didfe(), cntreg(), kmrec(), rdloc(), indgap() and the rest, 109 plots in all; bandx() is left to R, since its plot needs a statistic given as an R function), with the choices type, what, units and terms of those plots and the look of the R plots (black and grey, a black frame, a bold title; palette = "okabe" for colours, grid = TRUE for a grid). One drawing code in the C++ core serves every language.

  • plot() of synthc() and sdidx() draws the treated path solid and its comparison dashed, as plain lines, with a dotted line where the policy was adopted. plot(x, type = "o") puts a point mark on every period, as before.

  • Every package carries the title of the R package, “Statistical Toolkit for Criminology and Sociolegal Research”: the Python, JavaScript, Rust, Java and Go packages, the command’s manual page, the C header and the Homebrew, Scoop, Debian, RPM and container descriptions said “criminology and sociolegal statistics”. The README of the Python, JavaScript and Rust packages, which is what each registry shows, says how to cite crimlab.

  • Fixed: ecolrg(family = "negbin") on counts with no overdispersion. The search for the size sends it off without bound there, and past about ten million its score is no more than rounding; on 32-bit x86 without SSE2 (x87 arithmetic) a step taken from that noise ended at a wrong fit, with a lower likelihood. The search now ends at the cap once the size passes a million, where the fit is the Poisson fit to six digits. Results elsewhere do not change.

  • The tests of the command run on x87 as well: its test table compares the numbers inside a text result, and two cases whose last digits differ there have a bound.

crimlab 0.0.1

  • The results of the Indigenous health and wellbeing functions have plot() methods: gaps between groups with their intervals (indgap(), trchlthgap()), wellness beside distress (dualcont(), welprof(), holbal()), community indices and Community Well-Being scores (commidx(), cnscwb(), cwbscr()), standardised prevalence (stdprev()), ordered ratings (ordcmp()) and change between surveys (healchg()). A dot plot keeps every row label, in letters sized to the rows, and leaves room for its key above the data; lines over periods written as text (“2020/21”) are drawn in the order given and labelled as written.

  • Open data: odtab() loads a table of the project’s open data service by its key and odls() lists the tables, with their rows, columns and SHA-256. Everything about a table is read from the service’s manifest at the time of the call, so a table its publisher replaces is loaded as it is now, with no new release. A file is used only when its SHA-256 is the one the manifest lists; tables are kept in tools::R_user_dir("crimlab", "cache") while they still match. cols picks columns without regard to case or underscores, and base (or options(crimlab.data)) points at a mirror.

  • Placement volatility and alert complexity: plcvol() counts the changes of placement region in each person-year (within a record and between consecutive records) and alrtcx() the distinct alert configurations its records span, as defined in Ruhela’s study of Ontario’s restrictive confinement records. otpyr() reduces a release of those records (a data frame, or a key of the open data service read by odtab()) to one row per person and fiscal year, finding the columns without regard to case or underscores and taking the fiscal years from the data. cxvol() gives, pooled or for each fiscal year, the descriptives, the crude rate ratio, the one-to-one propensity matching, the count model with a random intercept per regional cluster and the bounds on the effect without ignorability; cxdml() the interactive double machine learning estimates (ATE and ATTE); cxyoy() the year-over-year table of regional changes per 1,000 placements and per 1,000 person-years with exact intervals. A single fiscal year with a year term, or a sample with no complex or no other person-year, is refused in words. cntmix() fits a Poisson or negative binomial count with a normal random intercept per cluster by the Laplace approximation, and cxsim() simulates the bias, spread and coverage of the estimators, with or without an unobserved confounder.

  • ctabx() bounds Cramer’s V right at any total: for a chi-square past about 1.5e6 (a 2 x 2 table of 1e8 counts) both bounds in R fell below the estimate, with warnings from R’s pchisq(), and on the command line and in Python the bounds took 149 s at 1e9 counts. R, the command line and Python now take them from one routine of the core, an integral of the noncentral chi-square whose work does not grow with the counts (about a millisecond a bound, to 1e-14 of references of 34 to 40 digits). With exact = TRUE the odds ratio of a 2 x 2 table and its interval are summed about their mode: a table of 1e6 counts took a minute.

  • pwranv() gives power 1 for a large effect (0.9999999486 at f = 1000) and returns at once for any f; f = 2^31 and larger never returned.

  • gstr() takes the same time whatever the counts: the binomial tail of its exposure test summed the terms one by one (20 s for counts near 2e6 with nsim = 0, no end for larger ones).

  • opteffort() gives finite efforts that add to the total for any total: from about 1e4 the multiplier underflowed and the first cell’s effort was Inf.

  • locgi(), olsdx() and sarml() give the same results for values shifted by a constant (and locgi() for values scaled): with values large next to their spread locgi()’s z-values moved by 0.4 (1e8) or became NaN (1e9), olsdx() moved its slope (1e6) or refused the column as collinear (1e7) and sarml() refused it (1e6).

  • gtwreg() fits an integer x with cons = FALSE (it stopped in R’s C words).

  • plothrz() refuses a period that is not finite; with one it never returned.

  • Refusals and warnings start with the function’s name, in the package’s words: about forty functions refused some inputs in base R’s words (a date where a column name goes, a function where a vector goes, text that is not valid UTF-8, a path in a folder that does not exist, a count past what can be allocated, a 1 x 1 matrix for a number), and the warnings of stdprev(), dosebin(), hetfx() and jntx() did not name their function. A text argument that is not valid UTF-8 is refused in R as on the command line (“ref holds text that is not valid UTF-8”); in Python with the same words. plotgain() no longer says that counts whose total overflows are all 0. A date or a time given where the scaling and IRT models take a count (burn, nsamp, ndim, maxit) is refused; it was read as its days or seconds since 1970 and ran for hours.

  • dktflw() takes its clearance intervals from the core’s beta quantile, as the command line does: R’s lost its digits, with warnings, once one count was 1e13 times the other.

  • Proofs: inst/lean/Volat.lean (the two measures: bounds, the cases of no change and of one record, relabelling, order of the records with a counterexample and the sorted case, adding a record, pooling, weighted and unweighted means, and two counterexamples on what alert complexity counts), inst/lean/Ident.lean (identification by adjustment, weighting and augmentation, double robustness, exact matching, the log-link rate ratio, a negative control, Manski’s bounds and the non-identification of the counterfactual arm) and inst/lean/Custody.lean (Lakner’s average daily population, length of stay and expansion estimator with the manual’s worked examples, and the arithmetic of year-over-year changes, including what a first-to-last column means once a year is added). proof() lists them.

  • odtab() gives the values the file holds: every column is read as text and becomes numbers only when each value is a plain decimal number held exactly, so identifiers such as "007", "7" and "0007" stay distinct and a column of "F" stays text (it became FALSE). A line with more or fewer fields than the header is refused, naming the line (a long line was wrapped into a row of its own), and so is a table whose number of rows is not the one the manifest lists. The manifest reader takes all JSON: an empty key, a string of any length (one of a few megabytes failed in PCRE), and characters past U+FFFF written as surrogate pairs.

  • Messages quote invalid UTF-8 bytes of the input as <xx>, in every refusal and warning of the package and of its C++ binding: dspbm(), clprep() and about twenty others carried the bytes themselves, and substr() or grepl() on such a message failed.

  • The keys that join several columns (the person-years of plcvol() and alrtcx(), the units and days of expjn(), smkiv(), ccross() and updwn()) no longer merge labels holding a carriage return: each value is escaped before the values are joined, so no label can imitate the join.

  • qltyrcd() reads its flags once: a vector of a million flags took minutes, copying a row per value, and is now read in a fraction of a second.

  • Arguments of the wrong type are refused in the package’s words, not base R’s: gtwreg() takes x = NULL (a model with the constant only, which stopped on its column names) and refuses a function or an environment as x; grdbin() a col that is not one name; xfrvrf() an imported that is not a vector; dagcol() a triple that is not labels; lrcce() an x that names no column; the plots a col that is not colours (a function was warned about, a data frame failed in the graphics).

  • The help of vrfpol() says what it refuses with an R error: only a poll that is not one pollutant name, as the command line refuses it; it said the function never stops with an R error.

  • bayout() gives R’s qnbinom() bound for every reference sum, in R, the command line and Python. For sums near 4,800 (a week of about 800) the probability of 0 was a subnormal number: the bound came out too low (805 for 856, raising alarms wrongly) and for nearby sums the search never ended (bayout(1:810) did not return). The quantile is now a search of at most about 160 evaluations of the distribution function, and the Poisson quantile of the command line and Python takes the same search.

  • vrfpol() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python, with the report R gives: the demo data are R’s draws, and the exposure file is read as R reads plain and gzip UTF-8 text. A bzip2 or xz file and UTF-16, UTF-32 or Latin-1 text, which R decodes, are an error report outside R.

  • New: tabrpt(), one call on a published table: catchk() on its groups, yoypx() on the change between periods, grprr() on the rates and trndrr() on each group’s trend.

  • New: ovrchk() flags the cells of a coded table of oversight reports that are not of the form of their field (a real date, a count, a flag) or of a pattern such as a case number.

  • New: ovrkwd() marks the reports that mention the words of keyword groups, whole words in any case, with a preset for mental health and race and any groups of one’s own.

  • New: ovrsoc() counts the subject officials of an oversight report by the first of six rules that applies (a roster, numbered tags, a plural, a singular mention, a statement of none) and says which rule and words gave the count.

  • New: ovrpar() codes police oversight reports into the fields of a schema (ovrsch()), by rules that are deterministic and offline, one row per report.

  • New: ovrsch(), the field schemas of oversight reports: each field read by a rule (text after a cue, a number, a date in the cue’s sentence, numbered tags, a flag and others), with a preset for the director’s reports of Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit.

  • New: ovrdte() reads the first date written out in a text, in English or French, as YYYY-MM-DD.

  • New: ovrtxt(), the plain text of a police oversight report’s page, with each block on a line of its own so that section headings stand alone; the first of the tools that code oversight reports.

  • New: synfix() draws example data in the shape of a published table: presets with the columns of Ontario’s corrections tables (segregation, deaths in custody, use of force), or any table given as the values of its columns. The draws are R’s after set.seed(), in every language.

  • New: pscred(), the credit for custody before sentence under s. 719(3) and (3.1) of the Criminal Code, at up to one and a half days a day, and the time left to serve.

  • New: olsdx(), least squares with the checks Algahtany, Kumar and Barclay (2022) report for their weather and crime regressions (standardised coefficients, tolerance and variance inflation, the Durbin-Watson statistic, leverage, studentised residuals and Cook’s distance) and the expected count, or a new month’s, at given weather.

  • Preset laniyonu-gent-cnt: the tract layout of Laniyonu (2018), stops on the three-level gentrification factor (the gent recipe) with the population as the offset and the crime and 311 controls, for cntreg().

  • New: dagcol(), the colliders of a directed acyclic graph given by its edges, shielded or not (v-structures), and whether a given triple is one.

  • New: tpsurf(), a thin-plate spline surface through values at points in the plane (Duchon 1977), smoothed by lam, on a grid with print() and plot() methods.

  • New: eofst(), the empirical orthogonal functions of a matrix of periods by places: spatial patterns, their series over time and the share of the variance of each.

  • New: prpmap(), a proportional symbol map: circles whose areas are proportional to the values, drawn largest first.

  • New: ptmap(), a point map in base graphics, with clusters from dbscn() or given, each in its own colour and shape with its number at its centre; dbscn() results now have a plot() method that draws them through it.

  • New: smmap(), small multiples of a choropleth map, one panel per period with the breaks and colours shared by every period.

  • New: chomap(), a choropleth map in base graphics from polygon coordinates, with no spatial package: quantile, equal or given class breaks computed in the compiled kernel.

  • New: gocoef(), the slopes of a gologt() fit laid out by threshold, with their standard errors and Wald tests.

  • New: gologt(), the generalised ordered logit (Peterson and Harrell 1990; Williams 2006): an intercept and slopes for each threshold of an ordered outcome, chosen covariates held parallel, with the Wald test of each covariate’s slopes and the likelihood-ratio test against proportional odds.

  • New: ulcate(), the U-learner of conditional average treatment effects (Kunzel et al. 2019) on the cross-fitted learners of dmlx(), with a final learner of its own and a clipped denominator.

  • New: xpshap(), the sampling Shapley values of Strumbelj and Kononenko (2014) for single predictions, with their standard errors.

  • New: xpale(), the accumulated local effects of one input (Apley and Zhu 2020), with the binning and centring of their ‘ALEPlot’.

  • New: xpcp(), ceteris paribus profiles: the prediction for single rows as one input moves over a grid.

  • New: xppdp(), the partial dependence of a prediction on one input (Friedman 2001) over an even or a quantile grid.

  • New: xpimp(), the permutation importance of a risk tool’s inputs (Breiman 2001; Fisher, Rudin and Dominici 2019), for an R function or the learners of suplrn(), with the shuffles drawn in the compiled core and returned.

  • New: mipmm(), multiple imputation of numeric columns by predictive mean matching in chained equations, with an analysis pooled by Rubin’s rules and the degrees of freedom of Barnard and Rubin, after mcartst().

  • New: rscchi(), the Rao-Scott test of independence in a two-way table from a stratified, clustered and weighted survey, first and second order and as an F, with the generalised design effects, beside svymx() and ctabx().

  • New: rcttml(), targeted maximum likelihood for a randomised trial with covariate adjustment (Moore and van der Laan 2009), for continuous and binary outcomes, beside the g-computation and the difference in means.

  • New: trnsp(), a trial’s average effect transported to a target population, or generalised to the population it came from, by the outcome model and by inverse odds weighting, with bootstrap errors.

  • New: gensw(), the sampling score of a trial against its target population and the weights that generalise or transport its units, with the logit standardised difference, Tipton’s generalisability index, the effective size and the covariate balance.

  • New: specrv(), the specification curve of Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson (2020): the treatment’s estimate for every outcome and every subset of optional covariates, with the joint inference of the median, the count significant and the summed t against permuted or bootstrapped null curves.

  • New: plntfx(), the recovery of planted effects: the outcome shuffled, an effect of known size added to the treated and the analysis run again, reporting bias, spread, coverage and rejection.

  • New: falsctl(), falsification with negative-control outcomes: the treatment’s coefficient on outcomes it cannot affect, with classical or HC1 errors, Kennedy’s permutation p-values and an adjustment for the number of controls.

  • New: pwrsim(), the power of a two-arm trial by simulation, for normal, binary or count outcomes, unequal arms and Welch’s or the permutation test, with its Monte Carlo error.

  • New: pwranv(), the power of the one-way analysis of variance from the noncentral F distribution, or the group size that reaches a given power.

  • New: blkprm(), the permutation test of a treatment effect with the assignment permuted within blocks, by enumeration or by draws, for the difference in means or the block-weighted difference.

  • New: rndalc(), randomisation lists by simple, permuted-block or stratified block randomisation from a seed, the same list in R and on the command line.

  • plotrdg() and plotvln() take their densities from the compiled kernel that the command line and the other languages use, so the curve is the same everywhere and on every version of R. The kernel agrees with stats::density() of R 4.3 and later to rounding.

  • New: cemtch(), coarsened exact matching (Iacus, King and Porro 2012) with the weights for the effect on the treated and the L1 imbalance, as Sampson and Winter (2018) match lead-exposed children.

  • New: lrcce(), the CS-ARDL long-run effects and adjustment speed from the unit estimates of ccepnl(), as Ditzen (2021) sets them out.

  • New: ifesc(), the generalized synthetic control of Xu (2017) on the interactive fixed effects model of Bai (2009), with staggered adoption, the number of factors by cross-validation and a bootstrap of units.

  • New: ppmlcf(family = "nb"), the control function with a negative binomial second stage and a cluster bootstrap of both stages, as Feigenbaum and Muller (2016) estimate lead’s effect on homicide.

  • New: ivfe(se = "dk"), the standard errors of Driscoll and Kraay (1998), robust to correlation across units and over time, as Batkeyev and DeRemer (2023) report them.

  • New: idwint() carries monitor readings to places by inverse-distance weighting of the nearest monitors and averages them by zone, as Rahman et al. (2023), Wongchanapai et al. (2025) and Wesselbaum (2022) assign exposure; gtwreg() is the geographically and temporally weighted regression of Kuo and Putra (2021), its bandwidth and time scale chosen by cross-validation or AICc; asrule() gives the association rules between two binned variables that Wongchanapai et al. (2025) mine with Apriori.

  • The command line computes the quantiles and medians of jntx(), ccross(ns =) and dosebin() as R’s quantile() and median() do, and the restricted cubic spline’s cube as a product in both, so that a spline surface of jntx() is the same fit in R and outside it (it differed by about 1e-8).

  • Fixed, after a review of the checks: ppmlfe() and ivfe() with se = "twoway" and other than two fixed effects, rddens() and rdloc() with fewer than 10 rows, rdloc() with a constant treatment, a refused row of polbrdarea() and an outcome polbrdn() lacks for PM2.5 are refused in words that name what is wrong; tailwd() refuses a negative speed and dwnexp(lonlat = TRUE) a latitude past 90; windiv() gives winds that cancel, and calm, no direction (NA); a whole number past 2147483647 is refused naming that limit; and the bin labels of invsn(), dosebin() and updwn() write Inf without a space, as the command line does.

  • Fixed: Python orrisk() refused or_, although an argument named as a Python keyword takes a final underscore elsewhere (from_, lambda_).

  • Fixed: inlhist() lost a value when the range of the values overflowed (c(-1e308, 1e308)); the breaks are now built from halves there.

  • windiv() with very narrow sectors builds its column names in less than half the time: each edge is formatted once.

  • ccross() takes a day column of ISO date text or of days since 1970-01-01, as the command line gives dates, and smkiv() reads ISO date text as dates, in R and on the command line alike; before, R’s ccross() refused numbers and the command line could not give smkiv() dates.

  • Fixed: irtem(), optcls(), dwnom(), cjrirt(), nomll(), irtlik() and nombt() accepted votes other than 1, 0 and NA, and a matrix of no votes; they refuse them now in the words of anomin(). ordocl() refuses a matrix of no responses, and a vector at once.

  • Fixed: clncolnms() could return repeated names (c("x", "x", "x_2") gave "x_2" twice); a number whose name is taken is now skipped. A tab inside a name is a word break, as the help says, and no longer deleted.

  • Fixed: mcartst() refused columns in different units (income next to a rate) as collinear; the rank check and the EM step’s eigenvalue floor are now on the scale of the correlations.

  • Fixed: rdloc(bw = "ik") and rddens() refused a running variable in metres or in thousands of kilometres; the bandwidths now scale with the running variable, and the estimates do not change.

  • Fixed: ppmlfe(), ivfe() and the other least-squares fits refused columns about 1e7 apart in scale as collinear; a column is now judged against its own size, and a column the fixed effects absorb is found by an explicit check in didfe(), wcbx() and the tests of ivfe().

  • Fixed: plot.lnkpr() returned an ROC curve of NA and an area of NA when some crimes were unsolved; the pairs with an unsolved crime are now left out, as lnkpr() leaves them out of its fit, and the area is the model’s AUC.

  • polrpttxt() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python: it writes the text of a vrfpol() report given as JSON, its numbers as R’s sprintf() and format() write them. vrfpol() itself runs in R only.

  • yoypdf() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python, writing the PDF R writes; without file the PDF is returned as text, and yoywr() there writes PDF too.

  • yoyhtml() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python, writing the page R writes; without file the page is returned as text, and yoywr() there writes HTML too.

  • prechk() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python, with the publishers’ codes of codes.tsv built into the command line as the presets are (cli/codes.sh writes cli/codes.inc, and CI checks it is up to date).

  • plotopt() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python, where no session keeps options: it checks the options given as R does and returns them with the defaults for the others.

  • plotevgrid() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python: its x maps each panel to a result of evtst() or stgdid(), or to the rows evtm, est, lo and hi themselves.

  • plothex() returns its hexagons in order of row, then column, in every locale (it ordered them by table() of text keys, which sorts in the session’s collation), and is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python with the same order.

  • co2fp() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python as the conversion it makes: the caller gives the wall and CPU seconds (and, where measured, the machine’s CPU accounting and the RAPL counters before and after) and gets R’s result without value. Timing an expression stays in R.

  • hwpwr() is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python. The result holds the rows R returns, the interval dt and the last reading as text (snap), which a later call takes as since; R keeps the last two as attributes.

  • plotrdg() and plotvln() are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python, returning the rows R returns (without the quartiles plotvln() keeps as an attribute). Their densities come from a kernel that reproduces stats::density(): the bandwidth rules nrd0, nrd, ucv, bcv and SJ, the binning, the FFT convolution and the interpolation, equal to R’s to rounding. In R both still call stats::density().

  • New: dwnexp() builds downwind-exposure instruments from sources of pollution and the wind: the sector and transport-wedge rules of Bao and Da (2026) for smoke plumes that move from day to day, and the angle and distance instrument of Ayesh (2023) for fixed sources. tailwd() gives the tailwind component along a flight course, from which Hener (2022) builds the instrument of the landing direction for aircraft noise.

  • New: invsn() takes by and rule to turn readings into one inversion per day, as Batkeyev and DeRemer (2023) require every three-hourly reading of a day to be inverted.

  • The help pages of windiv(), ivfe(), ppmlcf(), smkiv() and ccross() cite the designs of Karamik and von Graevenitz (2022), Sarmiento (2020), Batkeyev and DeRemer (2023), Hener (2022), Bao and Da

    1. and Rahman et al. (2023), with the arguments that reproduce each.

  • New: dirsim() draws compositions from a Dirichlet distribution (a gamma variate per part over its row sum), from R’s generator, so that set.seed() and rgamma() give the same draws; for testing a compositional analysis such as clrilr() before real measurements exist.

  • New: evlx() takes true, a true value other than the null to set the estimate against, as the argument of that name in the ‘EValue’ package.

  • Fixed: the second sweep found 25 more functions (lodimp(), lnroc(), ibench(), synexp(), bndxw(), rptvic(), etohlr(), mndla(), crchyp(), clrilr(), …) whose compiled readers asked for the length of NULL, a function or an environment; they now refuse it in words.

  • Fixed, after a second sweep: a function given as est to the exposure designs, end of a point datumpmap(), a list for the data of expconcidx(), exprspplr() and polbrdarea(), ref and a single p2 of jntx(), a bootstrap seed past an integer in the exposure estimators, an x of sarml() that is not numbers, an onlsmry() accumulator without its state, an infinite cnts of bandx(), a non-numeric source of advdif2d(), an object without a crs in crsof(), invalid text in pbbnd() and a table of no rows in yoysmry() used to fail in R’s words; each is now refused in the package’s, and ccross() names itself where it named plcday().

  • Fixed: kscan()’s Monte Carlo p-values used to depend on the order of the rows for a given seed (the times were shuffled over the rows as given); the shuffles now run over the incidents in the order of their coordinates and times. The p-values for a given seed change once; the clusters do not.

  • Fixed: ctabx() of a table of zeros used to print “n = NA” and give no statistics; such a table has no total, and it is now refused (here and on the command line).

  • Fixed, one function at a time: bufas() multiplied a factor or text r for its default buf before checking it (a warning or “non-numeric argument to binary operator”); gtmp() tested a function q for NA with a warning; the rgnmap*() checks turned a function into text; ppmlfe(), ppmlcf() and expgmm() converted a maxit past an integer with a warning; yoypdf() did not check lag; dstnskch(), rsvsmp(), relbl(), grdrcd() and grdlvls() took a function for their values or labels; crfno2(), crfpm25() and polbrdn() failed quoting a function as an outcome or pollutant. Each now refuses in its own words.

  • Fixed: a colour index past the range of an integer (col = 1e300, Inf) used to pass the plots’ colour check with a coercion warning, or fail in col2rgb() (“numerical color values must be >= 0”), in 12 plot functions; it is now refused as any bad colour (“col must be colours.”). A 1 x 1 matrix for a number such as bins used to be accepted with a recycling warning; it is now refused.

  • Fixed: a file path longer than a path can be (1e6 characters) used to reach path.expand() and its warning (“expanded path length … would be too long”) in co2fp(), raplok(), wrtxtfb() and the yoy*() writers; it is now refused, at most 4096 bytes.

  • Fixed: text that is not valid UTF-8 given for an argument used to stop 49 functions inside base R’s string functions (“invalid multibyte string”, “input string 1 is invalid UTF-8”) or, in a title, at the graphics device; the shared text check now refuses it first, naming the argument (bandx(), dstfit(), gplume(), fylbl(), the yoy*() writers, the descriptive statistics, the plots’ main, …), and a refusal that quotes such text shows its bytes.

  • Fixed: NULL, a function or an environment given for a vector argument used to reach the compiled code and fail there in R’s words (“LENGTH or similar applied to NULL object”, “cannot coerce type ‘builtin’ to vector”), in 31 functions (calaud(), fairdf(), tmpaud(), lodimp(), trnmat(), fairsim(), …); it is now refused in the package’s (“area must be a vector, got NULL.”).

  • New: ccepnl() estimates dynamic heterogeneous panels as Chudik and Pesaran (2015) set out: ylag lags of the outcome among the regressors, lags lags of the cross-section averages (by default the integer part of T^(1/3) when ylag > 0), the mean group estimator and its variance, and the half-panel jackknife (bias = "jack") or recursive mean adjustment (bias = "rma"), with the uncorrected estimate alongside in mg0. The pooled estimator is not made for dynamic models (pool), as their theory is that of the mean group estimator. Calls without the new arguments give the results they gave.

  • New: ccepnl() reports the heterogeneity-bias test of the pooled estimator of Juodis and Reese (2026, hb) and the number of factors the averages identify by their two regularized procedures (nfac), and offers the fixed-T variance of the pooled estimator of Brown, Schmidt and Wooldridge (2026, pvar = "bsw"). The help page sets out the five lessons of Juodis and Reese and what each asks of a user.

  • New: gmmpnl() returns the residuals in levels (resid), for Pesaran’s test of cross-sectional dependence and Moran’s I on each year, and the joint test as xtabond2 prints it (xwald); its help page maps each estimate and test of Andreatta et al. (2023) to a call and has an example of their specification on simulated data.

  • Changed: gmmpnl(small = TRUE) now makes the small-sample corrections as xtabond2 3.7.2 computes them (Roodman 2009): the conventional one-step variance and sigma2 times w / (w - k), the robust and two-step variances times (n - 1) / (n - k) G / (G - 1), and t and F on n - q - c or G - c degrees of freedom; it used n / (n - k) throughout. The joint test counts its degrees of freedom as the program does, with or without small. small = TRUE is refused with one group, or with no more transformed rows than coefficients.

  • Fixed: xcser() used to report r = 0 with an interval, p = 1 and nonzero cross-correlations for a constant series whose mean rounds (rep(1, 10), rep(0.1, 10)); a correlation with a constant series is undefined, and xcser() and the command line now refuse it, naming the series.

  • Fixed: the other statistics that divide by the spread of the data used to return numbers for a constant input whose mean rounds (rep(0.1, n), rep(1 / 3, n)), where they refused a constant with an exact mean: gearc(), lmorn(), locgi() and bvmor() (Geary’s C, local Moran, G and the bivariate Moran are undefined), txcal() (no calibration line), rdloc() (no Imbens-Kalyanaraman bandwidth), pcdtst() (a pair with a constant unit, now skipped) and the Jarque-Bera test of fepnl(). They now refuse it, or skip it, as for any constant. locgi(star = FALSE) gives NaN for the one unit whose value differs from all the others (its reference values are constant). cmpsc() gives no correlation to a stretch that does not vary, as cor() does, instead of one made of the rounding of its running sums. ecolrg() and evfilt() refuse a covariate column that does not vary (it cannot be told from the intercept), naming it, and evfilt() an outcome that does not vary.

  • Fixed: hsacc() used to break ties in the predicted score at the cut-off of top by the order of the rows, so that reordering the cells changed the hit rate, PAI, PEI and RRI (0.571 or 0.536 at top = 0.2 in one example); and nmax broke ties in density the same way. The new argument ties says which tied cells are hot: "in" (all, the default), "out" (none) or "frac" (each by the share of their area still needed); nmax takes the larger of equally dense cells first. The result no longer depends on the order of the rows; without ties at the cut-off it is as before.

  • Fixed: the point patterns and distance functions used to run without end, or until the machine was stopped, on extreme radii and magnitudes: a radius or distance of 5e-324 (ripk(), ripenv(), dbscn(), knxnr() and the other functions on the shared grid of points), a radius of 1e9 (ripk(), ripenv()), opteffort(W = 5e-324), dstfit() and yoypx() on counts of 1e50 and smixm() on coordinates of 1e200. The grid now starts from the smallest normal double and its searches stop at its edge; opteffort() refuses a W whose densities underflow or overflow; the goodness of fit of dstfit()’s discrete fits looks only at the jumps of the data; yoypx() refuses counts above 2^53 for its exact test; smixm() and sglmx() refuse points whose squared distances overflow; and the optimisers stop on an infinite start or search direction. Results for other inputs are unchanged.

  • Fixed: arimfc() and sarfc() used to refuse a series that does not vary once differenced (a constant, a straight line) in the optimiser’s words (“initial value in ‘vmmin’ is not finite”); they now say “y does not vary once differenced: the model has nothing to fit.”, as does the command line.

  • Fixed: the command line’s fylbl() converted an endyear of 1e300, Inf or NaN to a whole number with undefined behaviour; like R it now gives NA for a year outside the range of an integer. ousim() counted days / dt steps as an integer before checking them (1e16 at dt = 1e-9), and the periodic baseline of the Hawkes functions its integration steps; both are now counted in double first.

  • Fixed: the command line and clab_jrun() used to copy text that is not valid UTF-8 from an argument or a CSV cell into their output, which was then not valid JSON; they now refuse it, naming the argument, in the words of R (“group holds text that is not valid UTF-8.”). A NUL byte in a CSV cell used to end the cell’s number silently (4<NUL>0 was read as 4); it is now refused with its row and column.

  • Fixed: a function that calls another (runfx() calls exprun() and an estimator, plmfld() gplume(), polbrdn() crfno2(), rsvsmp() rsvidx(), xfrvrf() vrfmrg(), yoywr() the writers, and the exposure functions ppmlfe()) used to pass on the inner function’s refusals and warnings under the inner name (“gplume: …”); they now carry the name of the function called (ccross(), dosebin(), hetfx(), jntx(), lftab(), plcday(), plmfld(), polbrdn(), prechk(), rsvsmp(), runfx(), typefx(), xfrvrf(), yoyhtml(), yoywr()).

  • Fixed: the choice arguments of the exposure functions (ppmlfe(), ppmlcf(), ivfe(), ccross(), expgmm(), hetfx(), invsn(), jntx(), plcday(), rdloc(), smkiv(), typefx(), updwn(), windiv()) used to be refused by match.arg() in base R’s words (“‘arg’ should be one of …”); they are now refused like every other choice (“ppmlfe: se must be one of …”).

  • Fixed: hwpwr() used to report as measured a RAPL counter that fell by more than a wrap could explain (a reset read as 257 kJ) or read above its range, and read counter text that is not a whole decimal number (“0x10”, “1.5e3”, an embedded NUL, 26 digits); such rows are now not measured, with the reason in why. A FIFO in place of a counter used to block the call for ever; files are now read only when regular, opened without blocking. A library that is not NVML, or an nvidia-smi that fails, no longer adds a GPU row. dt is at most 604800 (a week) and pid at most 2147483647 (pid = 2^31 used to be accepted with a warning).

  • Environmental crime, with offences against the environment as the outcome: the LMDI decomposition of a count over the factors of a Kaya identity, over time and against a reference region (lmdix(), after Duan et al. 2026), the two-way fixed-effects regression of a count on drivers with an interaction, standardised coefficients, variance inflation factors, simple slopes and the Jarque-Bera test of the residuals (fepnl()), and Pesaran’s CD test of cross-sectional dependence (pcdtst(), as Andreatta et al. 2023 use it). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • Dynamic and heterogeneous panels, for the models Andreatta et al. (2023) fit to waste crime: difference and system GMM (gmmpnl(), Arellano and Bond 1991, Arellano and Bover 1995, Blundell and Bond 1998, with the instruments of Roodman 2009), one-step and two-step, first differences or forward orthogonal deviations, GMM-style instruments with lag limits and collapsing, IV-style instruments, the robust or conventional one-step variance and Windmeijer’s corrected or the uncorrected two-step variance, small-sample t and F statistics, a joint Wald or F test, the Arellano-Bond tests, the Sargan, Hansen and difference-in-Hansen tests and the instrument count; Wooldridge’s test of serial correlation (wsctst(), Drukker 2003); and the common correlated effects mean group and pooled estimators (ccepnl(), Pesaran 2006), on balanced and unbalanced panels, with a choice of the averages taken out. They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • Panels with a repeated unit and period are found by sorting the rows, not with a grid of units by periods, which for many units and periods could ask for more memory than the rows hold. pcdtst() and lmdix() refuse a panel whose units by periods pass 2^26 cells.

  • Spatial epidemiology and surveillance: Bayes outbreak detection (bayout()), exposure within a buffer and by kernel (bufexp(), kerexp()), the Leroux and BYM2 area structures (lerprc(), bym2sc()), ecological Poisson, negative binomial and zero-inflated regression with expected counts (ecolrg()), eigenvector spatial filtering (evfilt()), the metapopulation SIR model (spsir()), Weibull frailty and promotion-time cure models with CAR area effects (sfrail(), sfcure()) and the spatial encoding of graph attention (spbias()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • Geostatistics on planar coordinates: the empirical semivariogram (vgemp()), variogram models fitted by maximum likelihood (vgfit()), ordinary kriging (okrge()), block kriging (bkrig()) and its leave-one-out cross-validation (krigcv()), polynomial trend surfaces (trsurf()), the spatial linear model by profile likelihood (sglmx()) and the spatial linear mixed model by REML (smixm()), with a spatial data object (spobj(), spxy(), crsof()), the specification of a web map (lfspec()) and density-weighted sampling of points (spsamp()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • The energy and carbon footprint of a computation (co2fp()), modelled from running time, utilisation and memory (Green Algorithms) or measured from the CPU’s RAPL counters (raplok()), with the measured energy of other devices added from a table; the carbon intensity of electricity by location, offline (co2int(), co2inttab()), the location found without network access (dtctloc()) and everyday equivalents (fpeqv()). All but co2fp(), which evaluates an R expression, are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • Air pollution, for environmental criminology: the exposure-response estimate with a bootstrap sensitivity interval (exprspplr()), by the cross-fitted partially linear regression in the compiled core or any estimator with its interface, and the whole pollution-to-health pipeline from demo data, a (compressed) CSV or scalars to a report and its text (vrfpol(), polrpttxt()). exprspplr() with its built-in estimator is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python; the other two read files and write text in R.

  • Scaling and ideal points, for judges, courts, legislators and survey respondents: vote agreement (votagr()), Aldrich-McKelvey scaling (amscal()) and its Bayesian form (bamscl()), Basic Space scaling (bbscal()), classical, SMACOF and nonmetric MDS (cmdsf(), smacf(), nmdsf(), dblctr(), mdsfit()), Bayesian MDS and unfolding (bmdsf(), bunfld()), unfolding by least squares and by SMACOF (mlsmu(), smunf(), unfstr(), ipsrec()), INDSCAL (indscl()), Procrustes rotation (procrs()), NOMINATE utilities, likelihood, fit and bootstrap (nomutl(), nompr(), nomll(), dwnom(), nombt()), alpha-NOMINATE (anomin()), Optimal Classification and its ordered form (optcls(), ordocl()), binary IRT by EM (irtem()) and by Gibbs sampling (cjrirt(), irtlik(), irtpst()), ordinal and dynamic IRT (ordirt(), dynirt()), anchoring vignettes (anchv()), the bootstrap of scaling positions (scboot()), normal vectors and cutting lines (nrmvec(), cutlns()) and Wordfish (wrdfsh()). The samplers draw from R’s generator seeded as set.seed() (cjrirt() from Philox), so a chain is the same in every front end. All are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • Counts over time and across categories: ARIMA and seasonal ARIMA forecasts by exact maximum likelihood (arimfc(), sarfc()), the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck fit, simulation and Fokker-Planck density of a count series (ousim(), fpdens()), Lotka-Volterra rates of a yearly series (lvfit()) and the correlation of counts per unit between categories (catcor()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • Regression discontinuity: local-linear sharp and fuzzy estimates with the bandwidth of Imbens and Kalyanaraman (2012) or one given, three kernels, conventional and robust intervals (Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik 2014, with the pilot bandwidth equal to the main one), heteroskedasticity-robust or clustered errors and placebo cutoffs (rdloc()); the density test of McCrary (2008) (rddens()).

  • Exposure and crime, checked against the papers: the Newey-West lag of se = "nw" when lag is not given is now the automatic bandwidth of Newey and West (1994, equation 2.2) instead of their lag-selection parameter n, so results with that default change; two-way clustering gains the factor of each component (twc = "each") and the eigenvalue fix (psd = "eig") of Cameron, Gelbach and Miller (2011) in ppmlfe() and ivfe(). The first-stage table of ivfe() gains the Kleibergen-Paap rk statistic for several endogenous columns (it was NA) and the effective degrees of freedom and 5% critical value of the simplified test of Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013); the effective F itself was checked against their equation 3 and is unchanged.

  • ppmlfe() and ivfe() absorb any number of sets of fixed effects (a third set such as hour or region-by-year, which several of the papers use); one or two sets are computed exactly as before.

  • ccross() gains single-day lags (lagv, lag) and natural-spline controls (ns), the specification of the nationwide case-crossover study of Han et al. (2026), with a worked example of its main table.

  • smkiv(cf = "childs"): smoke PM2.5 as Childs et al. (2022) define it, PM2.5 above the three-year median of the same place and month on smoke-free days, on smoke days.

  • ppmlfe(se = "quasi"), the quasi-Poisson variance with the Pearson dispersion, the overdispersion adjustment Armstrong, Gasparrini and Tobias (2014) give for the case-crossover design of ccross().

  • ivfe() reports the Sargan statistic and the cluster-robust Hansen J of the two-step GMM estimate when there are more instruments than endogenous columns (overid, gmm), the cross-definition over-identification test the review of Yamada (2026) recommends.

  • ppmlfe(sep = "sst"): the check of Santos Silva and Tenreyro (2010) for Poisson estimates that do not exist, dropping the regressors that are collinear on the rows with positive counts. The iterative rectifier of Correia, Guimaraes and Zylkin, which drops rows instead, is not built: their 2020 paper names it without stating it.

  • Exposure and crime, a count with an endogenous exposure by the exponential-mean generalised method of moments of Mullahy (1997) and Windmeijer and Santos Silva (1997): multiplicative or additive residual, one-step, two-step or iterated weighting, cluster-robust errors and Hansen’s J (expgmm()).

  • Exposure and crime, the designs of 2019-2026: smoke instruments from plume data, raw or adjusted to the plumes that reached the ground (smkiv()); runs of exposed days and the effect by day in the run (exprun(), runfx()); effects by a moderator with the test of equality (hetfx()); the time-stratified case-crossover design (ccross()); two exposures together as a surface (jntx()); exposure in bins with tests of non-linearity (dosebin()); and effects by offence type with a multiple-testing correction (typefx()). Every choice the papers leave open is an option of the estimators, with the standard errors of each kind, the three first-stage statistics and the plug-in of the count instrument.

  • Exposure and crime, for counts by place and day against a daily exposure: Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood with one or two sets of absorbed fixed effects, an offset and one- or two-way clustered errors (ppmlfe()); two-stage least squares with the same effects and the first-stage Wald statistic (ivfe()); the Poisson control function with a cluster bootstrap (ppmlcf()); wind-direction and inversion instruments (windiv(), invsn()); the irrelevant-day placebo (plcday()); the upwind and downwind design around a road or a point source (updwn()); and the join of exposure to counts (expjn()). The methods are those of Bondy, Roth and Sager (2020) and of Herrnstadt, Heyes, Muehlegger and Saberian (2019, 2021).

  • Air pollution, for environmental criminology: Pasquill-Gifford dispersion coefficients (pgsig()), Briggs plume rise (briggs()), the Gaussian plume and puff (gplume(), gspuff(), the field plmfld()), an advection-diffusion grid (advdif2d()) and a particle walk (lagrprt()); the concentration-response functions of PM2.5 and NO2 (crfpm25(), crfno2()), the attributable fraction (attrfrac()), deaths avoided (mortdisp()), the burden of a population and of areas (polbrdn(), polbrdarea()) and the concentration index of exposure by income (expconcidx()).

  • Describing a table before trusting it: inline histograms (inlhist()), frequency tables (freqtbl()), pairwise correlations (cortbl(), topcors()), empty and constant rows and columns (drpempty(), drpconst()), clean column names (clncolnms()), multivariate outliers (mahaoutl()), the shape of missingness (missruns(), missgrid(), misspat(), misssmry()) and Little’s test of missing completely at random (mcartst()), duplicated rows (duprows()), a column report (profcols()), candidate distributions fitted by maximum likelihood and ranked by AIC (dstfit()) and Cochran’s Q for distinct groups before pooling (dstntst()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • One-pass summaries of data larger than memory: moment accumulators (onlsmry(), smryupd(), smrymrg(), smrystat()), reservoir sampling (rsvidx(), rsvsmp()) and the HyperLogLog distinct count (dstnskch(), dstncnt(), skchmrg()).

  • Search theory for search and rescue planning: lateral range curves (ltrlrng()) and sweep width (swpwdth()), the probability of detection from coverage (srchpod()) and of a parallel sweep with navigation error (pswppod()), the probability of success with Bayesian updating of containment (srchscs()), datum probability maps (datumpmap()), the optimal allocation of effort (opteffort(), optcrcsrch()), Frost’s optimal search squares (optsqr()) and the list of his book’s figures (srchfig()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • First Nations, Metis and Inuit health and wellbeing, a core part of the package beside the justice system it concerns: Statistics Canada’s published tables read with their quality flags (sctidy(), scests(), qltyrcd(), limfrom()), compared group by group and as whole rated scales (indgap(), ordcmp()), standardised by age (stdprev()), wellness beside distress (welprof(), dualcont(), holbal(), frmaud()), the First Nations Mental Wellness Continuum (mhcont()), healing as change (healchg()), connection across places (connassoc()), community-weighted indices (commidx()) and the Community Well-Being index (cwbscr()); the generations of residential school attendance and their dose-response (genexpo(), exptrnd()); the 2021 Census Indigenous Population Profile (cnsprof(), profshr(), cnsstd(), cnscwb()); and the Calls to Action (trcind(), trchlthgap(), trccmpl(), trcprog()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • polex() makes the simulated policy panel the examples of the policy functions use: twenty districts, 36 months and a staged reform with a known effect. The same seed gives the same panel in every front end.

  • thrtst(): when the quasi-Newton steps of the maximum-likelihood fit end short of the gradient criterion, up to 20 Newton steps now follow, so the fit converges on flat likelihoods on every architecture (arm64 builds reported the self-test’s fit as not converged). Fits that met the criterion give the same results as before.

  • thrtst() gains fit = "bayes": the threshold test fitted by Bayesian inference, as Simoiu, Corbett-Davies and Goel (2017) and Pierson, Corbett-Davies and Goel (2017) fit it, with a threshold for every group and area and the hierarchical priors that Simoiu et al. state, on the discriminant distributions. The posterior is sampled in C++ by the No-U-Turn sampler (chains, iter, seed), starting near the maximum-likelihood fit. thr gives the posterior means and intervals of the thresholds and of their differences from the reference group, and post the summaries, effective sample size and R-hat of every parameter. Chains with an R-hat of 1.05 or more, or fewer than 100 effective draws of a threshold, are refused. The fit agrees with Stan’s sampler on the same model. fit = "ml" stays the default. The two fits answer under different models and should be reported as such, not as checks of one another: with a threshold for every group and area under a hierarchical prior, on data made with one threshold per group the Bayesian fit can report thresholds far from the maximum-likelihood ones and from the generating values (three groups in ten areas, 20,000 stops a cell: about 0.13, 0.07 and 0.14 against 0.27, 0.20 and 0.31), which Stan reproduces on the same model.

  • thrtst() gains rank = "joint", the rank-order test of Anwar and Fang (2006) as the paper states it: the ranking of all officer groups is tested at once by their one-sided z statistics, and the null of no relative prejudice is rejected when the significant orders form a cycle; the common ranking is given otherwise. The pairwise form stays the default. With off, the new element mono holds their test of monolithic behaviour (Pearson’s chi-square of equal rates across officer groups, by group of the people stopped and measure).

  • ibench() gains the two methods of Ridgeway and MacDonald (2009) it left out: dr = TRUE gives the doubly robust benchmark (the propensity-weighted logistic regression of the outcome on the officer’s indicator and the circumstances, with a sandwich standard error), and local = TRUE Efron’s local false discovery rate of each officer, with the empirical null fitted as the package locfdr does by default (column lfdr, element null), flagging by it. Benjamini and Hochberg’s q stays. The defaults give the results as before. The tests check the doubly robust benchmark against glm() and a sandwich by hand, and the local rate against locfdr (reference values from dev/ref/lfdr.R).

  • lnsize() follows Malpass (1981) for esize: members nobody chose (null foils) leave the nominal size and the chance expectation, as Tredoux (1996, Table 4.2) shows. Before, esize did not adjust; that value is now esizeb. The two differ only when a member was never chosen. The interval of Tredoux’s E' (etrlo, etrhi) now takes the ends of the interval of I = 1 - sum p^2 to 1 / (1 - I), as Tredoux does, in place of a symmetric delta-method interval around E'; the ends move for every lineup (for 40 mock witnesses choosing 15, 5, 6, 4, 7 and 3 of six, E’ 4.44: from 2.98 to 5.90 before, 3.35 to 6.62 now). A choice of 0 records a mock witness who chose no one: it counts for psusp and fsize (as in Wells, Leippe and Ostrom 1979) and not for the spread of choices; nm is the number who chose a member. The tests reproduce the worked examples of Tredoux (1996, 1999).

  • lnroc() continues a curve that ends before far by the straight line to the point where every lineup counts as an identification, as pROC does, in place of a flat line; this changes pauc only when far is given above a procedure’s largest false alarm rate (the default never is). The tests reproduce Table 3 and the partial areas of Mickes, Flowe and Wixted (2012).

  • wdqx() now names the crimes prevented in the treated area and the buffer tne, the total net effect of Guerette (2009, Appendix B, equation 4), in place of net (same value), and adds the gross effect ge and the net effect ne of the same appendix. Its help page gives the formulas and Guerette’s worked example; the tests reproduce it.

  • Every result that holds something to draw has a plot() method on base graphics: estimates with intervals as dot-and-interval charts, effects by time since adoption, paths, survival and ROC curves, Lorenz curves, bars, matrices with their numbers in the cells, and surfaces. Each returns, invisibly, the data it drew. blpal() gives the colour-blind-safe palettes they share, plotopt() their session look and yoypals() the palettes of change tables; series differ in line type or point shape as well as colour. The general plots come with them: Lorenz and funnel plots (plotlrnz(), plotfnl()), distributions by group (plotrdg(), plotcdfs(), plotvln(), plothex(), plotgain()), series over time (plotcal(), plothrz(), plotmult(), plotbump()) and event studies in a grid (plotevgrid()). plot() of an hwkres result now returns the quantiles it drew.

  • Change tables from yoypx() (or any table with its columns) can be labelled (yoylbl(), fylbl()), summarised (yoysmry()) and written: CSV, TSV and JSON with every digit and every code as it is (yoycsv(), yoytsv(), yoyjs()), Markdown (yoymd()), a self-contained HTML page (yoyhtml()) and a PDF written by the package itself (yoypdf()), the format picked from the file name by yoywr().

  • The drift battery: the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (drftks()), the population stability index and Jensen-Shannon divergence (drftpsi()) and the chi-square tests of a categorical column against a known distribution and of two samples’ homogeneity (drftchisq(), drfthomog()), each result keeping its inputs in the attribute lakner. They check a new release of a published table against the last one before year-over-year change is computed from it. They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python (there without the Monte Carlo branch of drfthomog()).

  • rgnmapintg(), rgnmapcmp() and rgnmapalt() check a crosswalk from units to regions: each unit once and with a known region, a rebuilt map against the published one, and the map against an assignment by another route with the known disagreements named. They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • The categorical-integrity checks: codes decoded by an explicit dictionary or by their value labels (deccodes(), declbld()), recodes and relabels by name with every value mapped (grdrcd(), relbl()), declared levels (grdlvls()), a 0/1 indicator that refuses a factor (grdbin()), a recode proved by its cross-tabulation (vrfrcd()), counts checked against those a release published, with the label permutation that would explain a mismatch (vrfmrg()), and a variable checked after it crossed from one program to another (xfrvrf()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • shrs() gives each count’s share of a total in percent with Wilson’s score interval, from a vector or from a table summed by groups. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • toascii(), asciifb() and wrtxtfb() transliterate text to plain ASCII by a fixed table, keep valid UTF-8 as it is, and write text as UTF-8 bytes whatever the locale. They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • The summary statistics of the compiled core are exported: the mean, variance, correlation and standard deviation (cmn(), cvari(), ccorr(), csdev(), cdistm()), the normal density (cnormpdf(), cnormlpdf()), moments (cmom()), quantiles and robust spread (cqnt(), cmed(), cmad(), ciqr(), ctkyfnc()), trimmed and winsorized means (ctrmmean(), cwinsmean()), weighted moments (cwtd()), ranks (cspr(), cmidrk()), the covariance matrix (ccovm()), bootstrap means (cbootmean()), trimmed inverse- probability weights (cipw()), the incomplete gamma function (cgamcdf()) and splitmix64 uniforms (cunif()). They are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • prechk() checks a table against a preset before clprep() reads it, and names in one error every column the preset reads (directly, in a filter or in a recipe) that the table lacks, every label outside the codes the publisher lists for its column, and every label a mapping recode without a default does not cover. The codes of the Ontario segregation, restrictive confinement and deaths-in-custody tables are inst/presets/codes.tsv, from the ministry’s data dictionary; a preset of one’s own takes its codes as a data frame. The presets describe the layouts of published tables, and crimlab ships none of the tables.

  • The OTIS treatment-outcome presets of cbatt() (otis-a01-cbatt, otis-a01n-cbatt, otis-pa-cbatt, otis-pb-cbatt, otis-pc-cbatt) are tested against rmorie’s pair builders on a simulated placement table, with the values stored in tests/testthat/ref/preset.txt by dev/ref/preset.R.

  • hwpwr() reads the power and energy of the machine’s devices over an interval from the operating system’s own counters: RAPL on Linux, the NVIDIA management library, the amdgpu and Intel GPU hwmon files, the IOReport energy counters of Apple silicon, the Energy Meter Interface on Windows, and the battery while it discharges. Each figure says how it was obtained; an estimate carries its range, and a device that cannot be measured is listed with the reason.

  • mtrbnd() bounds the mean outcome under each of ordered sentences and the effect of each against the mildest, under the monotone treatment response and selection assumptions of Manski and Pepper. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • hsacc() scores a hot-spot map on later crimes: the hit rate, the predictive accuracy index, the predictive efficiency index and the recapture rate index. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • apcie() fits the age-period-cohort model of a table of counts by age and period with the intrinsic estimator of Yang, Fu and Land: the Poisson log-linear fit projected off the null vector of the design. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • spcure() fits the split-population (cure) model of Schmidt and Witte: a logistic share who would ever fail and a Weibull, exponential or lognormal time to failure among them, with covariates in both parts. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • lnkpr() links crimes into series: the distance, time and Jaccard similarity of behaviour of every pair, a logistic regression of being linked on them over the solved pairs, the area under the ROC curve of each, and the chance of a link for every pair. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • prohs() forecasts the risk of each grid cell from recent nearby incidents, weighted down with distance and age (Bowers, Johnson and Pease), and scores its hot cells on later incidents. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • wdqx() gives the weighted displacement quotient of Bowers and Johnson, with the counts expected after and the crimes prevented in the treated area and its buffer. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • rptvic() measures repeat victimisation: incidence, prevalence and concentration, the victims by number of victimisations against a Poisson count over the targets at risk, and the time between a target’s successive incidents. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • lnroc() gives the ROC curve of eyewitness identifications by confidence, the partial area with a bootstrap comparison of procedures, the diagnosticity ratio and the confidence-accuracy characteristic; lnsize() the fairness of a lineup from mock witnesses (functional size, Malpass’s and Tredoux’s effective sizes, the suspect’s share). Both are in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • ibench() benchmarks each officer’s stops against other officers’ stops in the same circumstances (Ridgeway and MacDonald), by propensity weights, with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate over the officers. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • thrtst() tests discrimination in searches three ways: the hit-rate test of Knowles, Persico and Todd, the threshold test with the discriminant distributions of Pierson, Corbett-Davies and Goel fitted by maximum likelihood, and a pairwise form of the rank-order test of Anwar and Fang. It is in clab_jrun(), the command line and Python.

  • gmixlr() now follows EuroForMix’s model where they differed: only the alleles seen are kept apart, every other allele (those of the reference profiles not seen among them) is one allele that does not stutter, sized as the largest size listed at the marker, and the degradation slope may exceed 1. Its log likelihood equals EuroForMix’s to 1e-6 at given parameters on eight cases and at the maximum on seven (one and two contributors, drop-out, drop-in, stutter, degradation, coancestry; dev/ref/efm.R); the rest is EuroForMix’s single precision.

  • cmpsc() now reproduces cmpsR exactly: a segment widened at the ends of the signature is cut, not moved; a lag counts when enough points overlap (so a segment may hang over the end of the reference); every confirmed peak is a candidate; ties are broken as cmpsR breaks them; and lags may fall on half points. full = TRUE keeps the earlier rule of lags wholly inside the reference. The scores, segments, lags and refusals equal cmpsR’s on 16 stored cases, edge cases among them.

  • pedlr(): the likelihood ratio of two pedigrees, given as tables of people and their parents, from DNA profiles at autosomal markers. The people not typed are summed over exactly by variable elimination on the alleles each received from each parent, so loops, inbreeding and any number of generations are allowed; mutation follows the equal or the stepwise model, with one rate or separate maternal and paternal rates. It equals kinidx() and patidx() where they apply, the enumeration of every allele in its tests, and pedprobr’s likelihoods.

  • gmixlr(): the likelihood ratio of two accounts of a DNA mixture by the gamma model of peak heights, with drop-out, drop-in, backward stutter, degradation and coancestry, the unknown contributors summed over and the parameters fitted by maximum likelihood under each account, or fixed with par. Its likelihood is checked against enumeration in R; the help page states the model’s assumptions and limits.

  • cmpsc(): the congruent matching profile segments score of two bullet signatures, with the multi-segment-length peaks of Chen et al. (2019). It follows the algorithm written out in R in its tests and is within one segment of cmpsR on simulated signatures.

  • clprep() reaches the command line, the Python package and the bindings through clab_jrun(), which does its recodes, filters and recipes in C++ with R’s messages and returns the generic’s arguments as args with the attributes of the R result beside them. Its preset table is cli/pre.inc, made from inst/presets/presets.tsv by cli/pre.sh; CI fails when the two differ. cli/test.tsv holds a case for every preset. Outside R, text is ordered by its bytes (R’s order under LC_COLLATE=C) and lowered as ASCII.

  • clab_jrun(), and with it the command-line program, the Python package and the bindings, now reaches every exported function: counts, rates and tables, the audits of risk scores, judges’ leniency, long stays, published figures and bands, stocks and flows, the Hawkes fits and other events in time, difference in differences, synthetic controls and the event study, surveys, few-cluster inference, the double machine learner and the super learner, and the spatial methods of near repeats, scans, densities, Moran’s I and spatial regression. A warning R gives is returned in the result as warnings, an array of its messages. lrpost(), impfpr() and lrcal() there now give one value as a number, not an array of one, as R does. src/dst.cpp adds the chi-square (central and noncentral), t, F, gamma, beta, Poisson and binomial distribution functions, upper tails and quantiles the front ends need; the R functions keep calling R’s own. The test of Ctrl-C in a running session measures the stop from the signal and sets the signal only once the call’s handler is in place, so a loaded machine no longer fails it.

  • The command-line program, the Python package and the Go, Rust, Java and JavaScript bindings now reach most of the package’s functions through clab_jrun(): fairness audits, trace evidence, aoristic weights and digit tests, sensitivity bounds, trajectory models, networks, the reporting checks, the spatial and hot-spot methods, spatial weights, toxicology, deterrence and severity, concentration and the dark figure, crosswalks and taphonomy, the learners, risk terrain and the life course, covariate balance, judge designs and Hawkes processes. Each reads its arguments with the R function’s checks and words and returns R’s result as JSON; cli/test.tsv holds the values of the R package for them (dev/clref.R). The normal quantile and distribution function the front ends need are kernels of their own (src/dst.cpp).

  • The tests no longer call other packages: the values of circular, DescTools, geosphere, geepack, igraph, MASS, sandwich, sf, spatstat, spdep, rmorie and rmoriebricklayer they compare with are stored in tests/testthat/ref, with the versions that computed them, by the scripts in dev/ref. Suggests now holds only testthat, knitr and rmarkdown. The ref workflow runs those scripts again every week on Linux (x86-64 and arm64), macOS (arm64 and Intel) and Windows, and fails when a value its platform’s packages give differs from the stored one by more than the tolerance of the test that uses it.

  • suplrn() stacks the learners of the package (least squares or logistic regression, the lasso, ridge and elastic net, the random forest) into a super learner: K-fold cross-fitted predictions, weights by non-negative least squares that sum to one, or the discrete super learner (the learner of least cross-validated risk), for numeric and 0/1 outcomes, the folds drawn from a seed and returned. With one learner the stack is that learner. dmlx() takes it as a nuisance learner (lrn = "stack", with stk, nstk and disc).

  • Ctrl-C (Esc in the R GUIs) now stops every long computation: the resampling, permutation, bootstrap and simulation loops, the iterative fits (elastic net, logistic and count regressions, EM, quasi-Newton, Weber point, k-means, power iterations, Louvain, synthetic control weights, fixed-effects sweeps) and the scans over pairs check for an interrupt every few milliseconds of work, free what they hold and end with R’s interrupt, never with a half-made result. In ‘Python’ the same loops raise KeyboardInterrupt.

  • etasf() fits the temporal ETAS model (marks and the modified Omori law), mvhwk() the multivariate Hawkes process of several types that excite each other, with its excitation matrix and spectral radius, and sthwk() the space-time Hawkes process of crime, with intensities at query points; hwksim() simulates from a space-time fit. proof("etasf") names the theorem that ties the Omori kernel to the Lomax kernel of hwkfit().

  • sdbsim() simulates the Short-D’Orsogna-Brantingham model of burglary hot spots, as agents on a lattice or as its reaction-diffusion limit with suppressed sites, and sdbthr() gives the linear stability of its uniform state: the threshold beyond which hot spots form and the fastest-growing wavelength. proof("sdbthr") and proof("sdbsim") name the Lean theorems on the steady state, the trace and the decay.

  • hypq() solves Larson’s hypercube queue of patrol units exactly (workloads, dispatch shares, lost or waiting calls, travel times) and sqrtlw() gives Kolesar and Blum’s square-root law of response distance; proof("sqrtlw") names its scaling theorems.

  • kmrec() gives Kaplan-Meier curves by group with Greenwood’s standard errors, survfit()’s log-scale intervals and medians, and the log-rank test; with unit it takes event times and studies the gaps between a unit’s events (repeat incidents at a place), the last one censored.

  • trndrr() measures the trend in a series of counts as a Poisson rate ratio per period (quasi-Poisson when overdispersed), by Mann-Kendall’s test (exact up to 8 periods) and the Theil-Sen slope, with the change on the period before and a test of equal seasonal totals; stpcp() finds a step change with its permutation p-value and Pettitt’s test; cusrv() watches counts by CUSUM; xcser() correlates two series, matched by period name, at lags as ccf() does.

  • hwkfit() fits a Hawkes (self-exciting) process to event times by maximum likelihood with the analytic gradient: exponential, Weibull or Lomax kernels, a constant baseline or a trend with a cycle, several of them compared by AIC, and the branching arithmetic (cluster size, stationary rate, share triggered) that proof("hwkfit") names. hwkres() gives the time-rescaling residuals with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of ks.test(), and hwksim() simulates the process, in time or in space and time, by its branching construction.

  • crsev() builds a severity-weighted crime index from counts by offence (the Crime Severity Index of Statistics Canada: weighted counts per population against a base, the weights given or made from incarceration rates and mean sentences); zcomp() ranks units on a composite of standardised counts across categories.

  • cconc() measures how concentrated a total is across units: the Gini coefficient and its exact split into the share of units at zero and the Gini of the rest, the Lorenz curve, top shares, dispersion against the Poisson, the bound chance alone allows and a simulated Poisson null, the Gini within groups, the urban-scaling exponent, and for the places of events in order the growth of distinct places. hilltl() estimates a power-law tail index: the discrete maximum likelihood estimate through the Hurwitz zeta function, or the Hill estimators, with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance of the fit. proof("cconc") names the Lean theorems on the split at zero.

  • crcap() estimates a hidden population from two lists (Lincoln-Petersen with its bounds over a box of list dependence, Chapman’s estimate with Seber’s standard error) or three (the never-listed cell under no three-way interaction, its sensitivity to that interaction, and the pairwise estimates); dkfig() bounds the dark figure of crime: the true victimisation rate under limits on a survey’s false positives and negatives with the breakdown point of a conclusion, the total when a survey covers only some offences, and the offences behind incidents counted under the hierarchy rule. proof("crcap") and proof("dkfig") name the Lean theorems.

  • bandx() reads band labels (“1-5”, “Over 60”, “Under 10”) into bounds, places a value in each band, expands a banded frequency table and shows how much a statistic depends on the cap assumed for an open band; pbbnd() gives the bounds a rounded or suppressed published cell allows and the envelope of the change between two published columns; yoypx() gives year-over-year (or any period) change within groups with the exact interval of the percent change, exact p-values adjusted for multiplicity, and the envelope that rounding allows. proof("pbbnd") names the Lean theorems on the envelope.

  • jdgiv() gives the judge-leniency instrument’s first stage, intention-to- treat effect and Wald ratio with the compliers’ effect over a grid of defier shares and effects, or the exact decomposition by type on a known population; jmono() gives each judge’s decision rate with a chi-square test of equal rates, the many-judge slope test of nested judges, and the comparison of judges within groups of cases with adjusted p-values and slopes; mmshr() gives the shares of sentences at, below and above a mandatory minimum. proof("jdgiv") and proof("jmono") name the Lean theorems.

  • agemix() gives the aggregate age-crime curve of a mixture of latent types and the covariance across types between ages that a single type forces to 0, with its permutation test on panel data; cumrsk() gives the cumulative risk of a first arrest, conviction or admission by age from a life table of first events, with Greenwood’s interval or with deaths competing; jpipe() gives rates between stages of the justice pipeline from window sums lagged by the time between the stages. proof("agemix") names the Lean theorem.

  • mndla() classifies segregation placements under the Mandela Rules (more than 15 days, or Rules 43 and 44 with hours out of cell) and gives the qualifying share by group over placements, people with any qualifying placement and people by their cumulative days, with exact intervals.

  • stkflw() relates person-days, the average daily population, admissions and the length of stay (any two give the rest) with changes, rates and the stock an earlier release removes; lostay() summarises lengths of stay, their bands and thresholds and the lognormal, exponential and Pareto fits; bklog() applies Little’s law to a docket; dktflw() gives clearance, rolling clearance, the pending caseload, Little’s law on published figures and the trend of the outcome mix; lftab() builds the actuarial life table; trnmat() gives the transition matrix between states with its stationary distribution. proof("stkflw") and proof("bklog") name the Lean theorems.
